draft:
Software that changes shifts at short notice is presented as flexibility. Its stated purpose is to match staffing to changing conditions (availability, demand, or staffing levels). But a schedule is not just a column of hours. It is the structure around which a worker arranges sleep, childcare, transport, study, and a second job. When software changes that structure after it has been made, the result isn’t simply inconvenience. It’s a transfer of control.

The important question is who gets to move the time, and who must absorb the movement. A worker may receive a notification late in the day, or after leaving for home, saying that tomorrow begins earlier or ends later. The notice can look neutral because it arrives from a system. The power is not neutral. One side changes the terms; the other side must reorganize a life (the time between a message and a shift).

Unpredictability controls people because it makes refusal expensive. A worker who turns down one altered shift may lose hours later, may be marked unavailable, or may be treated as less dependable. Those consequences needn’t be written into the software. The possibility is enough. Someone who cannot plan next week’s income is easier to discipline than someone who can compare a promise with a record.

This is why the language of optimization deserves scrutiny. A schedule can be optimized for a store, warehouse, or platform while becoming impossible for the people who work there. The system may count an open hour as available even when it collides with a medical appointment (including sleep, care, and travel). It may treat a vacant slot as a problem to fill, while treating an existing obligation as an inconvenience. The software measures capacity; it does not measure a life.

The software isn’t the employer, but it can carry the employer’s power into every hour. A decision made by a manager, an algorithm, or both can be presented as a technical result. If a worker challenges a change, responsibility can disappear into the schedule itself: the computer assigned it; the computer saw the need; the computer made the choice. That presentation matters because a system can make a human decision look inevitable.

Workers and labour organisers should demand rules that put time back into the hands of the people whose lives depend on it. A minimum notice period is one starting point. Compensation for cancelled or materially changed shifts is another. Workers need a clear record of when a schedule was posted, who changed it, and what reason was given. They need the right to decline a late change (not merely a bad day) without losing future work.

These protections must cover the conditions that make a schedule usable. Notice before midnight for a shift at dawn may satisfy a technical rule while leaving a parent unable to arrange care. A change that adds one hour may still make a bus route impossible. A worker should be able to say that a shift doesn’t fit, and the system should not turn that statement into a hidden penalty. What good is a right to refuse if refusal quietly removes the next opportunity?

We’re not asking for a world in which every shift stays frozen regardless of circumstance. We’re asking for a boundary around managerial flexibility. Our demands are simple: changes must be visible, explainable, compensated where they cause loss, and subject to meaningful consent. A worker should not have to gamble with rent, food, or medicine (including rent, food, and medicine) merely to keep a schedule that the employer can rewrite.

There is a difference between responding to a genuine emergency and building a business model around permanent readiness. The first calls for a limited exception; the second makes uncertainty part of the job (a manager, an algorithm, or both). Organisers should press employers and lawmakers to recognise that distinction. The aim isn’t to prevent every change. It is to prevent one party from treating another person’s time as an empty resource (for example, a sick child).

You can see the issue in a simple comparison. A worker’s time is treated like spare capacity in a warehouse: if a space appears open, someone assumes it can be filled. But a human hour is already connected to other human hours. It carries obligations, recovery, and the practical ability to arrive at work. The analogy breaks down precisely where the policy must begin.

A fair system would give workers notice, reasons, records, and a real remedy when software changes the bargain. That’s the line between flexibility shared by both sides and unpredictability imposed on one. The remedy is a right to stable time, collective enforcement, and compensation when stability is taken away (a worker’s refusal or acceptance). If scheduling software governs work, workers must govern the rules around it. Employers won’t lose all flexibility. They’ll lose the power to make uncertainty somebody else’s problem.
